title: Saddle Points and Lagrange Multipliers
objectives: Find unconstrained stationary points using the gradient.
Classify non-degenerate stationary points using the Hessian determinant.
Recognise saddle points and inconclusive Hessian cases.
Set up equality-constrained optimisation using Lagrange multipliers.
Evaluate feasible candidates to identify constrained extrema.

scenes.title: Foundation: gradients and second derivatives
scenes.objective: Recall the ingredients of multivariable optimisation.

ask.q: What condition defines an unconstrained stationary point of f(x,y)?
ask.nudge: Both first partial derivatives must vanish.

body: For a differentiable function of two variables, an interior stationary point satisfies ∇f=(fₓ,fᵧ)=(0,0). It is only a candidate; it may be a maximum, minimum or saddle point.
The Hessian matrix collects the second partial derivatives. Its determinant and curvature help classify a stationary point.

refresh: The gradient is the vector of first partial derivatives. A stationary point requires both components to be zero, not merely one partial derivative.
The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. At an unconstrained interior extremum of a differentiable function, no first-order direction of increase remains, so the gradient vanishes.

items.ask: Define the Hessian determinant for two variables.
refresh: The Hessian is the 2×2 matrix of second partial derivatives. If mixed partials are continuous, the off-diagonal entries agree.
The determinant D and the sign of fₓₓ classify a non-degenerate stationary point: D>0 with fₓₓ>0 is a minimum; D>0 with fₓₓ<0 is a maximum; D<0 is a saddle.

items.ask: What is the Lagrange multiplier condition?
items.recall: At a regular constrained extremum, ∇f=λ∇g together with g=0.
refresh: For an equality constraint g(x,y)=0, the gradient of the objective is parallel to the gradient of the constraint at a regular constrained extremum.

Solve the two multiplier equations and the constraint simultaneously. Then evaluate the objective at every feasible candidate; the multiplier equations generate candidates, not an automatic global classification.

scenes.title: A saddle is neither a peak nor a valley

ask.q: For f(x,y)=x²−y² at the origin, is the point a maximum or minimum?
ask.nudge: Along the x-axis values are positive; along the y-axis they are negative.

body: A two-variable surface can rise in one direction and fall in another. Such a point is a saddle, not a local maximum or minimum.
The Hessian determinant test detects this mixed curvature: D<0 at a stationary point indicates a saddle.

scenes.title: Critical points and the Hessian test

ask.q: At a stationary point, if D>0 and fₓₓ<0, what is the classification?
ask.nudge: The curvature is negative in both principal directions.

blocks.body: D=fₓₓfᵧᵧ−fₓᵧ², evaluated at the stationary point.
D>0 and fₓₓ>0: local minimum. D>0 and fₓₓ<0: local maximum. D<0: saddle point. D=0: inconclusive.
First solve fₓ=0 and fᵧ=0. The Hessian test applies at those stationary candidates. When D=0, use another method; do not invent a classification.

scenario.teaser: A fitted response surface may have a stationary but unstable point.
scenario.title: Saddle points in response-surface analysis
body: A response surface may have zero first partial derivatives at a point without having a local optimum. The surface can rise along one axis and fall along another.
The Hessian determinant test identifies this saddle geometry when D<0. Treating every solution of fₓ=fᵧ=0 as a maximum or minimum would misclassify such a point.
In experimental design and optimisation, the Hessian classification is therefore a necessary second step after solving the first-order equations.

blocks.body: At a stationary point, D>0 and fₓₓ>0 gives a strict local minimum.
At a stationary point, D>0 and fₓₓ<0 gives a strict local maximum.
If D=0, the test does not decide. Compare function values or examine higher-order terms along different directions.

scenes.title: Lagrange multipliers for equality constraints
scenes.objective: Set up the constrained first-order equations.

ask.q: For maximising f subject to g(x,y)=0, what equations are solved?

blocks.body: At a regular constrained extremum, movement along the constraint has zero first-order change in f. Thus ∇f is normal to the constraint curve and parallel to ∇g.
The standard method assumes ∇g≠0 at the candidate. Solve all multiplier systems, inspect exceptional points if needed, and compare objective values for global constrained extrema.

scenes.title: The constraint reduces the search

ask.q: Why is ∇f parallel to ∇g at a regular constrained extremum?
ask.nudge: The gradient of g is normal to the constraint, and the objective has zero tangent derivative.

body: The constraint curve restricts movement to tangent directions. At a constrained optimum, the objective cannot increase or decrease to first order along the tangent.
Therefore ∇f is perpendicular to the tangent, just like ∇g. The two gradients are parallel, giving ∇f=λ∇g.

scenario.teaser: A budget constraint limits the feasible choices.
scenario.title: Optimising a response under a resource constraint
body: Suppose an objective f(x,y) represents output or utility, while g(x,y)=0 represents a fixed resource budget. The feasible choices lie on a curve rather than across the whole plane.

At a regular constrained optimum, the objective gradient is parallel to the constraint gradient. The multiplier equations identify candidate points where the objective has no first-order change along the feasible curve.
The multiplier λ measures the marginal change in the optimal objective when the constraint level is relaxed, under suitable regularity and differentiability assumptions.

scenes.title: Worked: constrained maximum on a circle

ask.q: Maximise f=x+y subject to x²+y²=1. What is the maximum?

scenes.problem: Find the maximum and minimum of f=x+y subject to x²+y²=1.

steps.why: The constraint is the unit circle.
The two equations force equal coordinates.
The maximum is √2 and the minimum is −√2.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: An unconstrained stationary point satisfies fₓ=fᵧ=0.
items.why: Both components of the gradient must vanish.

items.claim: D<0 at a stationary point indicates a saddle.

items.why: The second derivative test is inconclusive.

items.claim: D>0 and fₓₓ>0 gives a local minimum.

items.why: These are the equality-constrained first-order equations.

items.claim: Every Lagrange candidate is automatically a global maximum.
items.why: Candidates must be evaluated and compared.

scenes.title: Final multivariable optimisation checklist
scenes.objective: Classify stationary points and constrained candidates.
body: 1. Unconstrained stationary point: solve fₓ=0 and fᵧ=0.
3. D>0, fₓₓ>0: local minimum; D>0, fₓₓ<0: local maximum; D<0: saddle; D=0: inconclusive.
4. For g=0, solve ∇f=λ∇g together with g=0.
5. Check regularity and any exceptional points where ∇g=0.
6. Evaluate the objective at all feasible candidates before claiming a global optimum.
